questions.text: A full-term infant delivered by cesarean section develops tachypnea, and a chest x-ray shows diffuse haziness with perihilar streaking. The symptoms resolve over the next 36 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (Type II RDS) from slow clearance of lung fluid
Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
Meconium aspiration syndrome
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

questions.text: A premature infant has recurrent apneic episodes. Which treatments are appropriate for apnea of prematurity?

answers.text: Theophylline, caffeine, CPAP, and stimulation
Surfactant replacement via the ETT
Prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency
Immediate high-frequency oscillatory ventilation

questions.text: A newborn's oxygen saturation and PaO₂ change rapidly regardless of incremental FiO₂ changes, and a pre/post-ductal saturation difference of 7% is noted. What process does this best describe?

answers.text: PPHN — PVR rises above SVR, shunting blood through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus after birth
Transient tachypnea of the newborn from retained fluid
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia from chronic ventilation
Retinopathy of prematurity from high oxygen exposure

questions.text: From a respiratory therapist's standpoint, which two mechanisms are the most important contributors to bronchopulmonary dysplasia?

answers.text: Atelectrauma (lung collapse) and volutrauma (large tidal volumes)
Surfactant deficiency and retained lung fluid
Subglottic and supraglottic airway swelling
Chloride ion transport failure and mucus plugging

questions.text: A term infant with meconium streaking is severely depressed at birth with gasping retractions and an APGAR of 4. What is the appropriate immediate intervention?

answers.text: Intubate and apply direct ETT suction (−70 to −100 mmHg) until no meconium is noted or after 2–4 aspirations, then place a clean ETT
Apply vigorous bag-mask ventilation immediately to clear the meconium
Administer surfactant before any suctioning
Place on CPAP at 4–6 cmH₂O and observe

questions.text: A ventilated preterm infant develops worsening V/Q mismatch and deteriorating ABGs from air dissecting into the interstitial space (PIE). What is the correct ventilator strategy?

answers.text: Lower airway pressures while maintaining gas exchange, ideally by switching to high-frequency jet ventilation
Increase PEEP and PIP to recruit the collapsed regions
Increase inspiratory time to improve distribution
Add prophylactic surfactant and increase FiO₂

questions.text: To reduce the likelihood of retinopathy of prematurity, what oxygenation target is recommended for a premature infant?

answers.text: PaO₂ less than 80 mmHg, with saturation maintained between >88% and <94%
PaO₂ of 80–100 mmHg, as in a term infant
Saturation greater than 95% at all times
FiO₂ of 100% to ensure adequate retinal perfusion

questions.text: Parents ask how to reduce their healthy infant's risk of SIDS. Which guidance is correct?

answers.text: Place the infant supine or side-lying and remove excess blankets and toys from the bed
Place the infant prone to reduce the risk of aspiration
Keep the infant warm with extra blankets during winter
Administer caffeine nightly to prevent apneic episodes

questions.text: A 3-year-old presents with a barking, seal-like cough and stridor. An A-P neck x-ray shows a steeple sign — narrowing of the trachea at the cricoid cartilage. What is the diagnosis and the usual cause?

answers.text: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), usually caused by the parainfluenza virus
Epiglottitis, usually caused by Haemophilus influenzae
Bronchiolitis, usually caused by RSV
Cystic fibrosis, caused by a CFTR mutation

questions.text: A child with epiglottitis is in the emergency department. Which statement reflects the correct understanding of this condition?

answers.text: It is supraglottic swelling shown by a thumb sign on lateral neck x-ray; only staff familiar with emergency intubation should manage the airway
It is subglottic swelling shown by a steeple sign and is managed with cool mist alone
It is a lower respiratory tract infection treated with RSV prophylaxis
It is best managed by repeated airway examination to monitor swelling

questions.text: A child with cystic fibrosis has salty-tasting sweat and recurrent pulmonary infections. Which underlying defect and diagnostic test correspond to this disease?

answers.text: A CFTR mutation affecting chloride ion movement, diagnosed with the sweat chloride test (iontophoresis)
Surfactant deficiency, diagnosed with the L/S ratio
An autosomal dominant defect in sodium transport, diagnosed by chest x-ray
RSV infection, diagnosed by viral culture
